question: Over the last few decades, cancer cases have slowly but steadily increased. In Austria, for example, the number of new cancer cases per year increased from 37 578 in 2001 to 39 737 in 2010. From 2011 to 2020, it increased further from 40 059 to 44 520, which can be explained by general demographic and health factors.

However, since 2021, there has been a clear and worrying acceleration in the rate of increase: The number of new cancer cases per year rose to 48 360 by 2024 – in just four years. Should this trend continue, some 54 000 new cancer cases per year could be expected in Austria by 2030. In addition, some oncologists and scientists report that cancer cases are becoming increasingly aggressive and developing faster.
In this context, the term ‘turbo cancer’ is sometimes used. 1.
How have cancer figures evolved in each Member State up to 2020 and since 2021?
Are there Member States which are ‘outliers’ in the statistics and have particularly high or low numbers of new cancers, and what are the reasons for this?
Can the Commission rule out that there is a link between the increase in new cancers, as well as the reports of ‘turbo cancers’, and COVID-19 vaccinations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.5.2026) Cancer incidence estimates and historical data for European countries are available in the European Cancer Information System (ECIS)1. The European Cancer Inequalities Registry2, a flagship of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan3, tracks cancer disparities in the EU, Norway and Iceland.

Its Data Tool integrates data from ECIS, whilst Country Cancer Profiles4 and EU Analytical Reports5 provide national analyses and EU-level comparisons. The reported number of new cancer cases grew across Member States up to 2020. This trend continued until 2022, when 2.78 million new cancer cases were estimated, a 2.4% rise from 2020. Since 2021, cancer incidence is stabilising or increasing moderately, with 2.

7 million new cases estimated in 2024. However, data enabling robust analysis from 2021 will become available in the second half of 2026, following the 2026 ECIS update where incidence data for 2021–2024 will be published. Cancer incidence varies between Member States, with Central and Eastern European countries generally showing higher rates.

However, in 2024 Denmark was estimated to rank highest for incidence (22% above the EU average) and Bulgaria lowest (26% below), in contrast to the general trend. These disparities likely stem from differences in prevalence of risk factors, population structures and ageing, existence and effectiveness of prevention and screening programmes, quality of diagnosis and treatment.

From the data registration perspective, quality and completeness of cancer registries also play a role. Finally, the Commission refers the Honourable Member to the answer to Parliamentary Question E-002078/202576, detailing that there is no scientific evidence of any increase of cancer occurrence following COVID-19 vaccination.
